analysis.one_liner: HAL is the government-owned company that designs, builds and repairs fighter aircraft, helicopters and aero-engines for India's armed forces.
analysis.whats_happening: HAL's Sept-2026 quarter (Q2 FY27) results came out on 12 November 2026: consolidated net profit rose about 16% year-on-year to roughly ₹1,936 crore on revenue from operations of about ₹7,613 crore (+15% YoY). But EBITDA grew only about 11.6% to ~₹1,739 crore, so the operating margin compressed, and the stock has underperformed the Nifty over the past 3 months (-4.4% vs +3.2%) partly on this margin softness.
analysis.plain_terms: This is a company almost entirely owned by the Indian government, making fighter jets, helicopters and engines mostly for the Indian Air Force and Navy. The tension: it has a huge, multi-year order book (media estimates put it around ₹2.5 lakh crore), but turning that paper into delivered aircraft and billed revenue has been slow — most visibly with the Tejas Mk1A fighter, where engines from General Electric have been delayed for years. Revenue is growing, but profit growth is now leaning partly on interest/treasury income rather than purely on the defence manufacturing business.
analysis.quarters: Q2 FY27 (quarter ended Sept 2026): revenue from operations ~₹7,613 crore (+15% YoY), EBITDA ~₹1,739 crore (+11.6% YoY), consolidated net profit ~₹1,936 crore (+16% YoY, versus ~₹1,669 crore a year earlier). Operating margin fell roughly 483 basis points quarter-on-quarter to about 22.85%, which several analysts attributed to higher employee costs. One notable flag: other income (largely interest on cash/advances) made up close to 38.5% of profit before tax in the quarter, meaning a meaningful chunk of profit growth did not come from the core defence manufacturing/servicing business.
analysis.performance_read: HAL did a 2-for-1 stock split on 28 September 2023, so any per-share price or dividend comparison that straddles that date is not on a like-for-like basis unless already adjusted — the figures and returns supplied here are already on a comparable basis. The stock is 12.4% below its July 2024 peak of ₹5,490.67, which is a pullback, not a crash — there is no demerger or spin-off in the corporate-action data to explain it. Over 1 year the stock is actually up 2.3% while the Nifty is down 2.8%; over 3 and 5 years HAL has massively outpaced the Nifty (+137% and +635% vs +28% and +39%), though it has lagged peer BEL over 3 years (137% vs 187%) while beating it over 5 years (635% vs 474%).
analysis.valuation_read: HAL trades around 33-36x trailing earnings, which is expensive in absolute terms. Why it's priced this way: very high returns on capital (ROE ~24%, ROCE ~32%), a scarce pure-play listed exposure to India's defence aerospace build-out, and a large reported order book giving multi-year revenue visibility. Whether it's actually cheap is a separate question — on the numbers it is not; the multiple already assumes smooth execution, and this quarter showed margin pressure and a rising reliance on non-core other income, both of which argue against calling it cheap today.
analysis.growth_read: Revenue growth (15% YoY) looks volume-led on the surface — more deliveries and servicing work — but margin did not keep pace (EBITDA +11.6%), so part of the growth is being absorbed by higher costs rather than flowing through to profit. The much-discussed Tejas Mk1A order, which would be a big incremental volume driver, has not yet meaningfully hit revenue because deliveries are still pending on GE engine supply.
analysis.health_read: HAL is reported as debt-free, so financial (balance-sheet) risk is low. The more relevant concern is business/execution risk: a rising share of profit before tax (~38.5% this quarter) came from other income rather than operations, and the company's own marquee programme (Tejas Mk1A) has been stuck for roughly two years waiting on a third-party supplier (GE) for engines despite HAL having built the airframes. Cash conversion of core operating profit, not solvency, is the thing to watch.
analysis.ownership_read: The promoter is the President of India (i.e., the Government of India), holding 71.64% as of September 2026, unchanged, with zero shares pledged. FIIs hold about 9.42%, DIIs about 12.56%, and public shareholders about 5.51%. There is no single well-known individual investor on the shareholding register — this is an institutional/government-held stock, not one associated with a marquee retail investor.
strengths: ROCE of ~32% and ROE of ~24%, with a debt-free balance sheet
Reported order book of roughly ₹2.5 lakh crore, several times trailing annual revenue, giving multi-year visibility
Q2 FY27 revenue from operations grew 15% YoY to ~₹7,613 crore
Zero promoter pledge and a stable 71.64% government shareholding
watchpoints: Operating margin fell ~483 bps quarter-on-quarter to ~22.85% in Q2 FY27 as EBITDA growth (11.6%) lagged revenue growth (15%)
Other income made up roughly 38.5% of profit before tax in Q2 FY27 — a meaningful part of profit is not coming from core defence manufacturing

Tejas Mk1A deliveries have been delayed since the original 2021 contract due to GE F404 engine supply shortfalls, with the first jet now targeted for around January 2027 — the headline order book has not been converting to revenue on schedule
At ~33-36x trailing earnings, the stock is priced for smooth execution; it has already underperformed the Nifty over the last 3 months (-4.4% vs +3.2%) following this quarter's margin miss
analysis.one_thing: Whether GE actually ramps up F404 engine deliveries and HAL hands over the first Tejas Mk1A to the Indian Air Force around the targeted January 2027 date — this is the clearest test of whether the large order book converts into delivered, billed revenue or stays execution-constrained.
analysis.data_notes: Q2 FY27 consolidated net profit (~₹1,935-1,936 crore, +16% YoY) and revenue (~₹7,613 crore, +15% YoY) are consistent across IANS, Daijiworld and Business Standard-style coverage. Set aside as outliers: a few syndicated headlines (Hans India, The Hawk, Social News) claiming a '16% drop' that contradicts their own body text and the clustered figures elsewhere, and separate figures from BusinessToday (~₹1,839 crore) and Elite Wealth ('+10.5% YoY'), which likely reflect standalone rather than consolidated results. Valuation ratios (P/E 33-36x, ROE 24%, ROCE 32%) are aggregator estimates (Screener/Trendlyne-style) and vary slightly by source — recommend checking Screener directly for the exact current print. The ₹2.5 lakh crore order-book figure is as reported in media and has not been independently verified against HAL's own filings.
